## Overview

We will cover:

::: {.incremental}

* Global explainability - what is the affect of this variable on the response?
  * Variable Importance
  * Partial dependence profiles
* Local explainability - Why was this observation predicted like that?
  * LIME
  * Counterfactuals
  * Anchors
  * Shapley values
    
    
:::    

## Black-Box Machine learning {.transition-slide .center}


## Black-Box Machine learning

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment}

**Interpretable Models**

::: {.incremental}

+ Logistic regression, LDA and (a single) Decision Tree are interpretable machine learning models
+ It is easy to see why any one observation was predicted the way it was (local)
+ and understand the effect any one variable has on the model's prediction (global)
+ In logistic regression and LDA this comes from looking at the model coefficients
+ In Decision trees we can look at the tree structure (as long as it is not too complex)


:::
:::
::: {.column .fragment}

**Un-Interpretable Models**

::: {.incremental}

+ Random Forests and Boosting models with many trees,
+ and Neural Networks with many hidden nodes or layers 
+ are not interpretable 
+ It is not obvious why any observation was predicted how it was
+ or what the affect of any variable was on the response variable


:::
:::
::::

## Tradeoff

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column .fragment}

::: {.incremental}

+ We need complex models to fit complex dataset
+ But the model is not being used by us (data scientists/machine learners)
+ It is used by some decision maker to help make a decision


:::
:::
::: {.column .fragment}

::: {.incremental}

+ They are unlikely to blindly trust you and use your model 
+ Saying it has a 0.95 out of sample AUC is unlikely to convince them
+ They will only trust your model if they can explain what it is doing


:::

:::
::::




## Local vs Global Explainability

::: {.incremental}

+ *Local*: Any question related to how a particular prediction for a particular observation was made;
+ *Why for this particular patient did the model recommend not to treat?*

:::

<br>

::: {.incremental}

+ *Global*: How the model behaves overall, or for a particular target feature of subset.
+ *How does certain increase in GDP would affect the labor rate?*

:::

## Global explainability {.transition-slide .center}
*How does certain increase in GDP would affect the labor rate?*

## Variable importance [(1/3)]{.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

Remember:

::: {.incremental}

- In Logistic regression and LDA (when we standardise the predictors) the larger the model coefficient the more important that variable for the prediction
- In DTs and RFs we had the gini index
- Importance from permutation

:::

<br>

::: {.fragment}

However

::: {.incremental}

- Effect of [collinearity]{.monash-orange2}


:::
:::

## Permutation variable importance [(1/2)]{.smaller}

::: {.fragment}

For trained model $\widehat{f}$, which depends on data ${\mathbf X}$ to predict response $y$, with loss function $L(y, \widehat{f})$ (e.g. misclassification rate, error),

:::

::: {.incremental}

1. Estimate $L(y, \widehat{f})$ on the data, $L^{\text{orig}}$.
2. For each variable $j \in {1, \ldots, p}$,
    - Generate data matrix ${\mathbf X}^{\text{perm}}$ by [permuting]{.monash-orange2} variable $j$. [This breaks the association]{.monash-blue2} between variable $j$ and observed $y$.
    - Compute the $L(y, \widehat{f})$ on the permuted data, $L^{\text{perm}}$.
    - Compare $L^{\text{orig}}$ and $L^{\text{perm}}$, e.g. $|L^{\text{orig}}-L^{\text{perm}}|$
3. Most important variables have larger values.    

:::

## Permutation variable importance [(2/2)]{.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column style="width: 40%; font-size: 80%;"}
Random forests have this baked into the model fitting (using the out-of-bag cases).

::: {.fragment}

Generally, should be conducted on the test set 9out of sample).

:::

<br>

::: {.fragment}

```{r}
# Using DALEX with tidymodels
# https://www.tmwr.org/explain
# https://ema.drwhy.ai/featureImportance.html
vip_features <- colnames(p_std)[2:5]

vip_train <- 
  p_std |>
  select(all_of(vip_features))

explainer_lda <- 
  explain_tidymodels(
    lda_fit, 
    data = vip_train, 
    y = p_std$species,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
vip_lda <- model_parts(explainer_lda,
                       B=100)
```
:::

:::
::: {.column style="width: 30%; font-size: 70%;" .fragment}

<br>
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 100%
vip_lda |>
  filter(variable %in% 
           c("bl", "bd", "fl", "bm")) |>
  mutate(variable = 
           fct_reorder(variable, 
                       dropout_loss)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=variable, y=dropout_loss)) +
    geom_quasirandom(alpha=0.5, size=1) +
    stat_summary(fun = "median", 
                 colour = "#D93F00",

```

## Partial dependence profiles [(1/2)]{.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

Partial dependence profiles show how the model prediction changes across different values of an explanatory variable.


::: {.fragment}

Computes 
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\hat{p}(Y = k \mid X_j = x) = \\
&\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \hat{p}(Y = k \mid X_j = x, X_{-j} = x_{i-j})
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::: {.fragment}

Where $x_{i-j} = x(x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{i, j-1}, x_{i, j+1}, \ldots, x_{ip})$

:::


::: {.fragment}

```{r}
# With DALEX
pdp_lda <- model_profile(
            explainer_lda,
            N=100)
```

:::


::: {.fragment}

Shows what the model sees.

:::

:::
::: {.column .fragment}

```{r}
#| label: PDP-lda
#| echo: false
#| out-width: 80%
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5.5
pdp_lda$agr_profiles |>
  rename(vname = `_vname_`,
         x = `_x_`,
         pred = `_yhat_`,
         species = `_label_`) |>
  mutate(species = str_remove(species,
           "model_fit.")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=x, y=pred, 
             colour=species)) +
    geom_line() +
    facet_wrap(~vname, ncol=2) + 
    xlab("") + ylab("predicted") +
    scale_color_discrete_divergingx(
      palette = "Zissou 1") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          legend.title = element_blank())
```
:::
::::

## Local explainability {.transition-slide .center}
*Why for this particular patient did the model recommend not to treat?*

## Why should I know about local explainers?

<br>
<br>

If you deploy a complex model, you [**may** need to be able to explain any decision]{.monash-blue2} made from it. 

<br>
<br>

::: {.fragment}

If the decisions affect people or organisations, they might be [challenged in court]{.monash-orange2}. You as the analyst may be expected to justify the decision, that it was made [fairly, without bias]{.monash-orange2}, and based on specific measurements collected for the model.

:::

## The goal

![](../images/LocalExplainability.png){width=80%}

## Global vs Local

::: {.incremental}

+ Linear models are global models, the affect of one variable is the same whatever the affect of the other variables 
$$
P(Y = 1\mid X) = \frac{1}{1+\exp(-\beta_0 - \beta_1x_1 - \beta_2x_2 - \cdots - \beta_px_p )}
$$
+ When the model is non-linear, the effect of different variables changes [locally]{.monash-orange2}
+ Take for example a decision tree
  + Iteratively split on a single variable
  + If first split on $x_1$ and then on both sides split on $x_2$, the effect of $x_2$ will be different depending on what $x_1$ was
+ The same can be said in NN's
  + Take the ReLU activation ReLU$(x) = \max(x, 0)$
  + One variable may causes a neuron to fire with some combination of the other variables, but with other combinations it may not
  

:::


## Linear vs non-linear separation

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
#| label: sine-curve-data
# Generate the more wiggly data
set.seed(1231)
x <- runif(3000, -1.2, 1.2)
y <- sin(2*pi*x)
d <- tibble(x, y)
ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_point(alpha=0.5)
rx <- cos(pi/4)*x - sin(pi/4)*y
ry <- sin(pi/4)*x + cos(pi/4)*y
rd <- tibble(rx, ry)
ggplot(rd, aes(rx, ry)) +
    geom_point(alpha=0.5)
set.seed(139)
x1 <- runif(3450, -2, 2)
x2 <- runif(3450, -2, 2)
cl <- ifelse(x2 > sin(2*pi*x1)/2, "A", "B")
rx1 <- cos(pi/4)*x1 - sin(pi/4)*x2
rx2 <- sin(pi/4)*x1 + cos(pi/4)*x2
dx <- tibble(rx1, rx2, cl)
ggplot(dx, aes(rx1, rx2, colour=cl)) +
    geom_point(alpha=0.5) +
  scale_color_discrete_divergingx(
    palette = "Zissou 1")
dx2 <- dx |>
  filter(rx1 > -1, rx1 < 1, rx2 > -1, rx2 < 1)
ggplot(dx2, aes(rx1, rx2, colour=cl)) +
    geom_point(alpha=0.5) +
  scale_color_discrete_divergingx(
    palette = "Zissou 1") +
  geom_point(data=rd, aes(x=rx, y=ry), colour="black")
dx2 <- dx2 |>
  rename(x1 = rx1, x2 = rx2)
write_csv(dx2, file="data/sine-rotated.csv")
```

## LIME

Fit a [linear regression in the local neighbourhood]{.monash-blue2} of observation of interest.

::: {.incremental}

1. Introduce distance $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ and calculate the distance between all features $x_i$ and $x_{i^{\prime}}$.
2. For each observation $i \in {1, \ldots, n}$,
    - Fit a linear model (logistic or linear regression ) estimating $\beta^{(i)}$ maximising the log-likelihood where the contribution of each observation $i^{\prime}$ is weighted by $w_{i^{\prime}} = \exp(-d(x_i, x_{i^{\prime}}))$
3. If the data is standardised the magnitude of the $\beta^{(i)}_j$'s tells us how important variable $j$ was to the prediction of variance $i$   

:::

::: {.column}

## LIME

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

::: {.fragment}

```{r}
#| results: hide
library(DALEXtra)
library(lime)
w_rf <- randomForest(cl~., data=w)
w_rf_exp <- DALEX::explain(model = w_rf,  
                        data = w[, 1:2],
                        y = w$cl == "A")
model_type.dalex_explainer <-
  DALEXtra::model_type.dalex_explainer
predict_model.dalex_explainer <-
  DALEXtra::predict_model.dalex_explainer
w_lime <- predict_surrogate(
  explainer = w_rf_exp, 
              new_observation = w_new[,1:2], 
              n_features = 2, 
              n_permutations = 1000,
              type = "lime")

```


::: {.fragment}

$P(Y = 1 \mid X) = \frac{1}{1+\exp(-\beta_0 - x_1\beta_1 - x_2\beta_2)}$

Class 1 = 'A' = Blue

:::

:::
:::
::: {.column}

::: {.fragment}

::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
w_lime_coef <- w_lime |>
  select(case, model_intercept, feature_weight) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename(x1 = feature_weight) |>
  mutate(x2 = 0)
w_lime_coef$x2[seq(1, 11, 2)] <- w_lime_coef$x1[seq(2, 12, 2)]
w_lime_coef <- w_lime_coef[seq(1, 11, 2),]
w_lime_coef
```

## Counterfactuals

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

::: {style="font-size: 60%;"}

Find the [closest observation (counterfactual)]{.monash-blue2} that has the [different class]{.monash-blue2}. 

::: {.fragment}

What values of the variables would you need to change to change the observation of interest into the counterfactual.

:::

::: {.fragment}

```{r}
library(iml)
# devtools::install_github("dandls/counterfactuals")
library(counterfactuals)
predictor_rf = iml::Predictor$new(w_rf, 
                                  type = "prob")
# predictor_rf$predict(w_new[1,])
w_classif <- counterfactuals::NICEClassif$new(
  predictor_rf)

w_new_cf <- w_new
w_new_cf$cl <- ifelse(w_new[,3]=="A", 
                           "B", "A")
for (i in 1:nrow(w_new)) {
  w_cf = w_classif$find_counterfactuals(
    x_interest = w_new[i,], 
    desired_class = w_new_cf[i,3],
                 desired_prob = c(0.5, 1)
  )
  w_new_cf[i, 1] <- w_cf$data$x1
  w_new_cf[i, 2] <- w_cf$data$x2
}
```

:::
:::

::: {style="font-size: 100%;" .fragment}
```{r}
#| echo: false
w_new_cf_all <- w_new |>
  rename(x1o = x1, x2o = x2, clo = cl) |>
  bind_cols(w_new_cf)

w_new_cf_all
```

:::

:::

::: {.column}
::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| label: cf
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: 80%
ggplot() +
    geom_point(data=w, aes(x1, x2, colour=cl), 
               alpha=0.6, shape=1) +
  scale_color_discrete_divergingx(
    palette = "Zissou 1") +
  geom_segment(data=w_new_cf_all, 
               aes(x=x1, y=x2, 
                   xend=x1o, yend=x2o,
                   colour=cl),
            linewidth=3, alpha=0.5) +
  geom_text(data=w_new, aes(x1, x2, colour=cl, 
                            label=1:6),
            size=4, fontface="bold") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {style="font-size: 40%;"}
<center>
Note: If case is misclassified, the desired class needs to be the true class.
</center>
:::

## Anchors

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
How far can you [extend from the value of the observation in each direction]{.monash-blue2} and still have all observations be the same class.

::: {.fragment}

How big is a rectangle that contains each observation and only other observations of the same class

:::


::: {style="font-size: 60%;" .fragment}

<br><br><br><br>
Note: No working R package to calculate these.
:::
:::

::: {.column .fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: 80%
w_anchors <- data.frame(
  xmin=c(-0.6, -0.05, 0.18, -1, -0.65, 0.1),
  xmax=c(-0.3, 1.0, 1.0, -0.2, 1.0, 0.8),
  ymin=c(-0.25, 0, -1, -0.2, -1, 0.4),
  ymax=c(1, 0.15, 0.15, 1, -0.5, 0.6),
  cl=c("A", "B", "B", "A", "B", "A"))
ggplot() +
    geom_point(data=w, aes(x1, x2, colour=cl), 
               alpha=0.6, shape=1) +
  scale_color_discrete_divergingx(
    palette = "Zissou 1") +
  geom_rect(data=w_anchors, 
               aes(xmin=xmin, ymin=ymin, 
                   xmax=xmax, ymax=ymax,
                   colour=cl),
            linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.5,
            fill=NA) +
  geom_text(data=w_new, aes(x1, x2, colour=cl, 
                            label=1:6),
            size=4, fontface="bold") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Shapley values

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

Intuitively, a variable is important if the model's predictions change a lot if I take that variable away 

<br>

::: {.fragment}

Let $g(X_1, \ldots, X_p)$ be the machine learning model

:::

::: {.fragment}

Then variable $j$ is important for observation $i$ if 
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\left|g(x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{ip})\right.\\
&\left.- g(x_{i1}, \ldots, x_{ij-1}, x_{ij+1}, \ldots, x_{ip})\right|
\end{aligned}
$$
is large

:::

:::
::: {.column .fragment}

However, if variable $j$ is correlated with another variable then it can be important and this distance can look small

<br>

::: {.fragment}

Therefore we need to consider the model with an without variable $j$, alongside all other combinations of the variables

:::

::: {.fragment}

e.g. 

$$
\left|g(x_{ij}\cap x_{iS}) - g(x_{iS})\right|
$$
where $S$ is all subsets of $\{1, \ldots, p\}\setminus j$

:::

::: {.fragment}

Averaged across all sets $S$ is a Shapley value

:::




:::
::::

## Shapley values

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

A Shapley value is computed from the [change in prediction when all combinations of presence or absence of other variables]{.monash-blue2}. 

::: {.fragment}

In the computation, for each combination, the prediction is computed by substituting absent variables with their average value.


```{r}
#| eval: false
library(kernelshap)
library(shapviz)
w_explain <- kernelshap(
    w_rf,
    w_new[,1:2], 
    w[,1:2],
    verbose = FALSE
  )
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: false
save(w_explain, file="data/w_explain.rda")
```

:::

:::
::: {.column .fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 7
#| out-width: 70%
load("../data/w_explain.rda")
w_shap <- w_new |>
  mutate(shapAx1 = w_explain$S$A[,1],
         shapAx2 = w_explain$S$A[,2])
```

## Summary

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

Which variable is most important?

|obs | expect | LIME | CF | SHAP |
|----|--------|------|----|------|
| 1  | x2     | x1   | x2 | x1   |
| 2  | x1     | x1   | x1 |x1, x2|
| 3  | x1 x2   | x2   | x1 | x2   |
| 4  | x1, x2 |x1, x2|x1, x2|x1, x2|
| 5  | x1, x2 | x2   |x1, x2|x1, x2|
| 6  | x1     | x2   | x1 | x2   |
:::
::: {.column .fragment}
They don't all agree.
<br>
<br>

::: {.fragment}

You [need good visualisation of the model in the data space]{.monash-orange2} to fully digest the importance of the variables.

:::

<br>

::: {.fragment}

NOTE: We can use [magnitude]{.monash-orange2} when interpreting the local explainers because we used [standardised data]{.monash-orange2}. The interpretations are more complicated otherwise.

:::

:::
::::

## Example: penguins [(1/2)]{.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

Compute SHAP values for the neural network model

```{r echo=FALSE}
#| message: false
set.seed(821)
p_split <- p_std |> 
  initial_split(prop = 2/3, 
                strata=species)
p_train <- training(p_split)
p_test <- testing(p_split)

p_train_x <- p_train |>
  select(bl:bm) |>
  as.matrix()
p_train_y <- p_train |> pull(species) |> as.numeric() 
p_train_y <- p_train_y-1 # Needs to be 0, 1, 2
p_test_x <- p_test |>
  select(bl:bm) |>
  as.matrix()
p_test_y <- p_test |> pull(species) |> as.numeric() 
p_test_y <- p_test_y-1 # Needs to be 0, 1, 2

```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| eval: false
library(keras3)
#p_nn_model <- load_model_tf("../data/penguins_cnn")
p_nn_model <- keras3::load_model("../data/penguins_nn.h5")
p_nn_model

# Explanations
# https://www.r-bloggers.com/2022/08/kernel-shap/
library(kernelshap)
library(shapviz)
p_explain <- kernelshap(
    p_nn_model,
    p_train_x, 
    bg_X = p_train_x,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
p_exp_sv <- shapviz(p_explain)
save(p_exp_sv, file="../data/p_exp_sv.rda")
```


::: {.fragment}

Highlight SHAP values for a misclassified Gentoo penguin

:::

:::
::: {.column .fragment}
```{r}
#| echo: false
library(keras3)
#p_nn_model <- load_model_tf("../data/penguins_cnn")
p_nn_model <- keras3::load_model("../data/penguins_nn.h5")


p_train_pred <- p_nn_model |> 
  predict(p_train_x, verbose = 0)
p_train_pred_cat <- levels(p_train$species)[
  apply(p_train_pred, 1,
        which.max)]
p_train_pred_cat <- factor(
  p_train_pred_cat,
  levels=levels(p_train$species))

```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| crop: true
#| out-width: 80%
load("../data/p_exp_sv.rda")
p_exp_gentoo <- p_exp_sv$Class_3$S
p_exp_gentoo <- p_exp_gentoo |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(species = p_train$species,
         pspecies = p_train_pred_cat,
  ) |>
  mutate(error = ifelse(species == pspecies, 0, 1))
library(ggpcp)
p_exp_gentoo |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo") |>
  pcp_select(1:4) |>
  ggplot(aes_pcp()) +
    geom_pcp_axes() + 
    geom_pcp_boxes(fill="grey80") + 
    geom_pcp(aes(colour = factor(error)), 
             linewidth = 2, alpha=0.3) +
  scale_colour_discrete_divergingx(palette="Geyser") +
  xlab("") + ylab("SHAP") +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.fragment}

Note: the SHAP values for misclassified penguins are much lower than values for all other penguins on `bm` and are higher than `bl`. i.e. `bm` is less important and `bl` is more important for those observations' prediction 

:::

:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

Weights from hidden layer

```{r}

p_nn_wgts <- keras3::get_weights(p_nn_model, trainable=TRUE)
p_nn_wgts[[1]]
c("bl", "bd", "fl", "bm")
```

<br>

::: {.fragment}

Model uses mostly `bl` and `bm`.

:::

::: {style="font-size: 60%;" .fragment}

<br>
Note: this analysis used the [training set]{.monash-orange2} because this Gentoo penguin was misclassified as an Adelie in the training set.

```{r}
#| echo: false
table(p_train$species, p_train_pred_cat)
```
:::

:::
::: {.column .fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: 70%
# Check position on bm
shap_proj <- p_exp_gentoo |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo", error == 1) |>
  select(bl:bm)
shap_proj <- as.matrix(shap_proj/sqrt(sum(shap_proj^2)))
p_exp_gentoo_proj <- p_exp_gentoo |>
  rename(shap_bl = bl, 
         shap_bd = bd,
         shap_fl = fl, 
         shap_bm = bm) |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(p_train_x)) |>
  mutate(shap1 = shap_proj[1]*bl+
           shap_proj[2]*bd+
           shap_proj[3]*fl+
           shap_proj[4]*bm)
sp1 <- ggplot(p_exp_gentoo_proj, aes(x=bm, y=bl, 
             colour=species, 
             shape=factor(1-error))) +
    geom_point(alpha=0.8) +
  scale_colour_discrete_divergingx(palette="Zissou 1") +
  scale_shape_manual("error", values=c(19, 1)) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(aspect.ratio=1, legend.position="bottom")
sp2 <- ggplot(p_exp_gentoo_proj, aes(x=bm, y=shap1, 
             colour=species, 
             shape=factor(1-error))) +
    geom_point(alpha=0.8) +
  scale_colour_discrete_divergingx(palette="Zissou 1") +
  scale_shape_manual("error", values=c(19, 1)) +
  ylab("SHAP") +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(aspect.ratio=1, legend.position="bottom")
sp2 <- ggplot(p_exp_gentoo_proj, aes(x=shap1, 
             fill=species, colour=species)) +
  geom_density(alpha=0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = p_exp_gentoo_proj$shap1[
    p_exp_gentoo_proj$species=="Gentoo" &
    p_exp_gentoo_proj$error==1], colour="black") +
  scale_fill_discrete_divergingx(palette="Zissou 1") +
  scale_colour_discrete_divergingx(palette="Zissou 1") +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(aspect.ratio=1, legend.position="bottom")
sp2 <- ggplot(p_exp_gentoo_proj, aes(x=bm, y=bd, 
             colour=species, 
             shape=factor(1-error))) +
    geom_point(alpha=0.8) +
  scale_colour_discrete_divergingx(palette="Zissou 1") +
  scale_shape_manual("error", values=c(19, 1)) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(aspect.ratio=1, legend.position="bottom")
sp1 + sp2 + plot_layout(ncol=1, guides = "collect") &
  theme(#legend.position="bottom",
        legend.direction="vertical")
```
